slides.title: Dryer vent cleaning
slides.body: Property managers carry the fire liability and hate sourcing it. Recurring contract, a van, and about $400 of tools.

slides.title: Post-construction cleanup
slides.body: Small contractors subcontract this on every job and complain about finding anyone reliable. Ask three builders this week.

slides.title: Pool equipment repair
slides.body: Everyone competes on cleaning. Almost nobody does pumps and heaters, which bill at a far higher rate.

slides.title: Menu photography per dish
slides.body: Delivery apps rank listings with photos. Owners know it and still will not shoot them. Price per plate, not per hour.

slides.title: Estate sale listing
slides.body: Heirs will not photograph and list 200 items. You do the work, you take a percentage, they never touch a keyboard.

caption: None of these need a following, an app, or a pitch deck. They need a phone and someone willing to make the first ten calls. Which one would you actually do?

hook: 5 Signs Your Business Idea Is Bad

slides.title: You cannot name one buyer
slides.body: Not a demographic. One person, with a name, who could pay you this week. If they do not exist, neither does the business.

slides.title: Your 'why now' is just AI
slides.body: AI is how you build it, not why anyone needs it. If removing that word kills the pitch, there was no pitch.

slides.title: It needs both sides at once
slides.body: Marketplaces are useless until both sides show up. You are signing up for two businesses, not one.

slides.title: The pitch needs a diagram
slides.body: If you cannot say it in one sentence, a stranger scrolling past will not decode it either.

slides.title: You dread the selling part
slides.body: Excited to build, dreading to sell, is the most common way this ends. Selling is the job.

caption: Most ideas do not fail because they were wrong. They fail because nobody stress-tested them for an afternoon first. Which of these have you been ignoring?

hook: 5 Truths About Starting No One Says

slides.title: Your idea is not the moat
slides.body: Willingness to do sales is. Two people with the same idea get completely different outcomes for this reason alone.

slides.title: First customers already know you
slides.body: They come from your contacts, not from ads. Ads are for scaling something that already converts.

slides.title: You will change it in 60 days
slides.body: Plan for the pivot instead of pretending it will not happen. Build the cheap version you can afford to throw away.

slides.title: Revenue before logo
slides.body: Naming, branding and a website are procrastination wearing a suit. Take money first.

slides.title: Money changing hands is the only proof
slides.body: Not compliments. Not sign-ups. Not 'I would definitely use that.' Only payment.

caption: Every one of these is obvious in hindsight and ignored in practice. Save this and reread it the week you launch. Which one stings the most?

hook: 5 Businesses You Can Start With A Van

slides.title: Junk removal
slides.body: People pay to make a problem disappear today. You need a van, a dolly, and the number of your local tip.

slides.title: Furniture assembly
slides.body: Flat-pack arrives, nobody wants to build it. Flat fee per item, two hours a job, no inventory.

slides.title: Mobile car detailing
slides.body: You go to the office car park and work through the row. One customer becomes eight without moving.

slides.title: Pressure washing
slides.body: Driveways, patios, shopfronts. The before-and-after sells itself, which makes it the easiest thing to market.

slides.title: Retail display swaps
slides.body: Brands pay someone to change the display in shops on a route. Boring, contracted, repeats monthly.

caption: Every one of these is a van, a skill you can learn in a weekend, and the willingness to knock on doors. Which one is closest to what you already own?

hook: 5 Questions To Kill A Bad Idea Fast

slides.title: Who is bleeding right now
slides.body: Not who would find it nice. Who has the problem badly enough to be searching for a fix this week.

slides.title: What do they use today
slides.body: If the answer is nothing, that is usually because the problem is not worth solving, not because you are first.

slides.title: How do I reach ten of them
slides.body: If you cannot name a group, forum, trade body or list where they gather, marketing will cost more than you think.

slides.title: What breaks if I charge double
slides.body: If demand vanishes at a real price, you have a hobby with extra steps.

slides.title: Can I test it this week
slides.body: If the smallest honest test takes three months, shrink the test, not your standards.

caption: Answer these on paper before you write a line of code. Most ideas die at question two, which is the cheapest place for them to die. Which one do you skip?

hook: 5 Things To Sell That Are Not Products

slides.title: Access
slides.body: A vetted group, a directory, an introduction. People pay to skip the search, not for information.

slides.title: Done-for-you setup
slides.body: Software is cheap and confusing. Charge to configure the thing other people already bought.

slides.title: A recurring audit
slides.body: Monthly check of something that quietly breaks: listings, backups, pricing, reviews. Low effort, high anxiety.

slides.title: Speed
slides.body: Same service everyone offers, delivered in 24 hours. Urgency is a feature people will pay a premium for.

slides.title: Accountability
slides.body: Not the plan, the follow-up. Coaching is mostly someone checking whether you did the thing.

caption: None of these need inventory, a warehouse, or a supplier. They need one clear promise and someone who keeps it. Which would you buy?

hook: 5 Cheap Ways To Test An Idea

slides.title: Sell it before it exists
slides.body: One page, a real price, a real checkout. If nobody clicks buy, you just saved six months.

slides.title: Do it by hand first
slides.body: Deliver the service manually for five customers. You learn what to automate instead of guessing.

slides.title: Post where they already are
slides.body: Describe the problem in the forum they use. If the thread goes quiet, that is your answer.

slides.title: Ask for a deposit
slides.body: Interest is free. A small deposit is the cheapest honest signal you will ever get.

slides.title: Count the competitors
slides.body: Zero is a warning, not an opening. A few profitable rivals means the money is real.

caption: Every one of these costs under a hundred and takes under a week. Building first costs months and tells you less. Which would you try first?
